icd10_codes.description: Displaced bimalleolar fracture of left lower leg, initial encounter for closed fracture
Other fall from one level to another, initial encounter
Other wilderness area as the place of occurrence of the external cause

dialogue:
[doctor] hi there , {PATIENT_FIRST} . i'm doctor {DOCTOR_LAST} , one of the orthopedic surgeons . how are you doing ?
[patient] hanging in there . this boot thing they put on me is not comfortable .
[doctor] yeah , that's a splint . we'll talk about that . so i have the notes from urgent care in {CITY} , but i'd like to hear it from you . what happened ?
[patient] so on saturday my son {OTHER_FIRST} and i were hiking up {PLACE} . it was just a day hike for fun , we're both off on weekends . we were about two hours up the mountain trail , above the tree line , where it's all loose rock and scree .
[doctor] okay .
[patient] and there's a spot where the trail goes along a ledge , and the edge just gave way under my left foot . i slid off the ledge and dropped down maybe five or six feet onto the rocks below .
[doctor] wow . okay . and how did you land ?
[patient] i landed on my left foot , and it twisted under me , like my foot went out and my leg kept going . i heard a crack . then i kind of rolled down a few more feet .
[doctor] okay . did you hit your head ?
[patient] no , i had my pack on and it kind of cushioned me . no head injury .
[doctor] okay , good . any loss of consciousness ?
[patient] no .
[doctor] okay . and how did you get down ?
[patient] that was the hard part . {OTHER_FIRST} called search and rescue , and they came up and carried me out on a litter . took about four hours . then he drove me to the urgent care , and they did x-rays and put me in this splint and told me to see you .
[doctor] okay . and the pain right now ?
[patient] it's about a six out of ten , throbbing , both sides of the ankle . worse when i put it down .
[doctor] okay . any numbness or tingling in your foot ?
[patient] no , i can feel my toes .
[doctor] okay . have you been putting any weight on it ?
[patient] no , i've been using the crutches they gave me .
[doctor] good . what about other medical problems ?
[patient] i'm pretty healthy . i do n't take any medicines . i do n't smoke .
[doctor] okay . any prior surgeries ?
[patient] just my appendix when i was a kid .
[doctor] okay , and what do you do for work ?
[patient] i'm an electrician , so i'm on my feet and on ladders all day .
[doctor] okay , that's going to be a factor in your recovery . all right , let me take a look . i'm going to take the splint down so i can see the ankle .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] so , on exam of the left ankle , there's significant swelling on both the inside and the outside , with bruising . there are some fracture blisters starting here on the inside , but the skin is intact , no open wounds . you're tender over both the medial malleolus and the lateral malleolus . i'm not going to move it much . your foot is warm , your dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable , and you can feel me touch the top and bottom of your foot . can you wiggle your toes ? good . your calf is soft .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] so let's look at the x-rays from urgent care . hey dragon , show me the left ankle x-rays . okay , so you have a fracture of the fibula on the outside , right at the level of the joint , and a fracture of the medial malleolus on the inside . so that's what we call a bimalleolar fracture . both pieces are displaced , and the ankle joint has shifted a little bit to the outside , meaning it's unstable .
[patient] so what does that mean ?
[doctor] so , my assessment is that you have a displaced bimalleolar fracture of the left ankle from a fall from a ledge while hiking . because it's displaced and the joint is unstable , this is something we fix with surgery , what we call an open reduction and internal fixation , where we put the bones back in place and hold them with a plate and screws .
[patient] okay . when would that be ?
[doctor] we want the swelling to come down first , so the skin is healthy enough to operate through . usually that's about seven to ten days . in the meantime , i want you to keep it elevated above your heart as much as possible , toes above your nose , and ice it . we'll put a new well padded splint on today . strictly non weight bearing with the crutches .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] for the pain , you can take ibuprofen and tylenol , and i'll give you a small supply of oxycodone for the worst of it . and i want you on a daily aspirin to help prevent blood clots while you're not walking .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] after surgery , you'll be non weight bearing for about six weeks , then we'll get you into a boot and physical therapy . so realistically you're looking at three months before you're back on ladders .
[patient] and hiking ?
[doctor] hiking on rough terrain is probably more like four to six months .
[patient] okay . well , better to fix it right .
[doctor] exactly . we'll see you back in one week to check the skin and schedule surgery .
note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT

Left ankle fracture.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

{PATIENT_FIRST} {PATIENT_LAST} is a {AGE}-year-old male referred from urgent care in {CITY} for a left ankle fracture. On Saturday, he was on a recreational day hike on a mountain trail above the tree line when the edge of a ledge gave way and he fell approximately 5 to 6 feet onto rocks below, landing on his left foot with a twisting injury. He heard a crack. No head injury or loss of consciousness. He was carried out by search and rescue. X-rays at urgent care showed a fracture and he was placed in a splint. He reports 6/10 throbbing pain about both sides of the ankle. He denies numbness or tingling. He has been non-weight bearing on crutches.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY

None. Appendectomy in childhood. No medications. Nonsmoker.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Electrician, on his feet and on ladders.

PHYSICAL EXAM

Left ankle: Significant medial and lateral swelling with ecchymosis. Early fracture blisters medially. Skin intact. Tenderness over the medial and lateral malleoli.
Neurovascular: Foot warm. Dorsalis pedis pulse palpable. Sensation intact to light touch dorsally and plantarly. Toes move freely.
Calf soft and nontender.

RESULTS

X-rays of the left ankle demonstrate a displaced fibular fracture at the level of the syndesmosis and a displaced medial malleolus fracture with lateral talar shift, consistent with an unstable bimalleolar ankle fracture.

ASSESSMENT

Closed displaced bimalleolar fracture of the left ankle, sustained in a fall from a ledge while hiking on a mountain trail during leisure activity.

PLAN

Discussed operative management with open reduction and internal fixation once soft tissue swelling allows, anticipated in 7 to 10 days. Placed in a well-padded splint today. Strict non-weight bearing with crutches. Elevation and ice. Ibuprofen and Tylenol, with a limited supply of oxycodone for breakthrough pain. Aspirin daily for VTE prophylaxis. Return in 1 week for skin check and surgical scheduling. Expected return to work in approximately 3 months.
